segments.text: When you type a message to chat GPT, you're using words, and it responds with words.
But underneath, AI doesn't read it that way. It splits your text into small pieces called tokens.
Underneath each of those tokens is an embedding, a row of numbers that represents its starting
meaning. But words don't exist in a vacuum. To show how AI connects them,
we'll use whole words to make things easier to see. This board leaves out the two big problems
context must solve, different meanings, and pronouns. Let's look at the left side, problem one.
The same word can mean something completely different depending on the sentence. If you say,
please turn on the light, light means brightness. But if you say the empty suitcase felt light,
it means not heavy. So when you type light, how does the AI know which version you mean?
Now look at the right side, problem two, pronouns.
The cat was thirsty, so it drank the milk. Here it means the cat. But in the sentence,
the milk was fresh, so the cat drank it. It means the milk. When you use a pronoun like it,
how does the AI know what you're actually referring to? The answer is right there in the
rest of the sentence. The surrounding words help AI figure out the meaning. Are human brains
use those surrounding words to lock on to the right meaning almost instantly.
But for earlier AI, keeping that context connected was a serious challenge,
because it read text strictly in order, one word at a time.
This diagram shows how earlier AI read text. It steps through the sentence chronologically,
arrow by arrow. By the time it reaches the word it, at the bottom, it's a long way from cat.
Because it processed sequentially, earlier AI often struggled to keep that connection
in longer passages. That difficulty brings us to a major breakthrough.
In 2017, eight researchers at Google published a paper called attention is all you need.
It introduced an architecture called the transformer, which is actually the T in chat GPT.
This diagram shows how that architecture reads. Instead of word by word, the complete message
arrives together, processed at once. Because every word is visible at the same time, the pronoun
it can look back and draw directly on cat, regardless of how many words sit in between.
But pulling out the right meaning requires a bit of math. There's more to reading than taking
in the words. AI actually needs to figure out which words matter most and use that information
to update the underlying numbers. This graphic shows how that happens.
Attention weighs information from relevant words and blends it into the target token's numbers,
like the arrow from it back to cat. Next, transformation uses learned patterns to further
process those blended numbers, physically changing their shape. Together, they update each token.
Let's return to our examples to see how the transformer resolves ambiguity.
For problem one, surrounding words guide the math. Turn on tells the AI light means brightness,
while empty means not heavy. For pronouns, thirsty points it to the cat,
and fresh points it back to the milk. By evaluating the relationships between these words,
attention and transformation help AI work out which meaning fits. Because the model
weighs the whole sentence, rather than reading strictly literally, this is the same process that
helps AI interpret sarcasm and idioms. We've seen how the AI figures out which words matter,
but there is one catch. Processing everything simultaneously destroys the sequence of the
sentence, and the words alone aren't enough. Their order matters too.
Here is how a transformer keeps words in order. Consider the simple sentence, dog bites man. If we
swap the words to man bites dog, we have the exact same three tokens, with the exact same starting
embeddings, but the order carries an entirely different meaning. Look at the panel on the left.
Without position information, the model has the words, but they float in a scattered cloud.
It cannot tell which word came first. The solution is on the right.
Position stamps. By assigning a numbered position, one, two, and three, to each token,
the model preserves the grammatical sequence, even when it analyzes all the words at exactly the
same time. This technique locks the sequence in place. Positional encoding tells the transformer
where every token belongs. Attention is all you need. AI uses relationships between words
to help interpret your message.
